mcqs.question: Why must origin egress capacity be sized for the miss-rate tail rather than the average miss rate?
options: Because a small percentage-point jump in miss rate against a catalog this large translates into an order-of-magnitude spike in absolute origin load during unusual events
Because origin storage is billed at a flat monthly rate regardless of traffic
Because edge caches never actually reduce origin load in practice
Because regional demand skew has no effect on origin traffic
mcqs.explanation: At catalog scale, moving from 2% to 10% misses is a 5x jump in absolute origin requests, not a small change — sizing only for the average leaves no headroom for that spike. Origin egress is usage-based, not flat-rate; edge caches are exactly what keeps average miss rate low; and demand skew is a direct driver of which titles miss where.

mcqs.question: What is the main operational cost a team accepts when moving from single-CDN to multi-CDN with real-time routing?
options: Losing the ability to serve any cached content during normal operation
Managing multiple provider integrations and a routing layer whose decisions need to be trusted and debugged
Being unable to use a CDN for video at all
Guaranteed higher latency for every request, in every region
mcqs.explanation: Multi-CDN's real cost is operational: more integrations, more dashboards, and a routing layer that itself becomes a critical system to trust and debug. It doesn't disable normal caching, doesn't preclude CDN use, and doesn't guarantee worse latency — done well it often improves latency by routing around a degraded provider.

mcqs.question: A title goes unexpectedly viral and many edges miss it simultaneously. What technique at the regional tier prevents this from becoming an origin-overloading thundering herd?
options: Rejecting all requests for that title until an engineer manually intervenes
Permanently caching every title at every edge to eliminate misses entirely
Increasing the title's price to reduce demand
Request collapsing — the first miss fetches from origin once while concurrent misses for the same title wait on that single in-flight fetch
mcqs.explanation: Request collapsing turns many simultaneous misses into a single origin fetch, which is exactly what prevents a thundering herd. Rejecting requests or manual intervention isn't a design, permanently caching everything everywhere is the over-provisioning this system explicitly avoids, and pricing has nothing to do with cache architecture.

mcqs.question: Why is routing every viewer to the geographically nearest edge, by distance alone, a pitfall?
options: The nearest edge could be degraded or lack the title in cache, so proximity alone can route viewers into a slower path than a slightly farther but healthy, cache-hot edge
Geography is completely irrelevant to playback latency
Distance-based routing is technically impossible to implement
Edges are never actually placed based on geography in the first place
mcqs.explanation: Proximity is a reasonable default but not sufficient on its own — a nearer edge that's degraded or missing the title can be slower in practice than a farther, healthy, cache-hot one. Geography does matter for latency in general, distance-based routing is common and implementable, and edges genuinely are placed with geography as a factor — the pitfall is treating it as the only factor.
